newsitem.title: USA: "Tax Freedom Day" on May 9 this year-policy group.
newsitem.headline: "Tax Freedom Day" on May 9 this year-policy group.

text.p: Americans on average will work until May 9 to pay off their total tax bill this year, two days more than in 1996, a tax policy group said Monday.

The 1997 "Tax Freedom Day" set a record in the annual study by the Tax Foundation, primarily due to steady economic growth that pushed some people into higher tax brackets and subjected them to a bigger tax bite, the group said.

The Tax Foundation projected the average American would have to work 128 days to pay off total federal, state and local taxes this year. In 1996, which was a leap year, "Tax Freedom Day" arrived on May 7, the group said.

"If the economy's going to grow and you're going to have a progressive tax system, then Tax Freedom Day, however you measure it, is going to go later ... each year," J.D. Foster, executive director at The Tax Foundation, said. "It's one of the consequences."
The Tax Foundation projected that federal, state and local taxes will be $9,205 for the average American this year and average income will be $26,187.

Starting with 1993, Tax Freedom Day has steadily arrived later, according to the study. "This year the average American has to work a full week longer than in 1993 to pay his or her tax bill," the group said.

Another budget policy group said the Tax Foundation's analysis was incorrect and accused the group of trying to inflame public distress around tax time by releasing its study the day before the income tax filing deadline of April 15.

"Their figures misuse the data and exaggerate both the tax burden of the typical family and the extent to which the typical family's taxes are rising," Robert Greenstein, executive director of the Centre on Budget and Policy Priorities, said.

Greenstein said the study's use of average family income is skewed by the wealthy and suggests a bigger tax bite than the "typical" family experiences. The typical family would be the median, one that falls in the middle of the income spectrum, he said.

"By releasing the report on April 15, they foster a misleading impression that the typical family is working for months to pay the federal personal income tax, when in fact the typical family works three weeks only until Jan. 20 to pay the federal income tax," Greenstein said.
The Tax Foundation does its calculation by taking figures from the Census Bureau and dividing total taxes by national income.
By state, New York had the latest tax freedom day of May 23, driven by high state and local taxes, Foster said. Connecticut came next, followed by the District of Columbia.
Louisiana had the earliest, April 24, followed by Tennessee, Alabama and Arkansas.
Income in each state is a key to its ranking "so Connecticut, which has a fairly late tax freedom day -- that's driven largely by the very high incomes in the state," Foster said.

"We need to change the trends that the Tax Foundation has shown us these last five years -- four straight years of increasing the tax burden on Americans," Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, said.
"The time has come to stop increasing taxes and to start increasing jobs, opportunity and growth for Americans everywhere," he added.
